function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: This function generates a Dockerfile in the specified directory with basic configuration. The Dockerfile will be tailored to a simple Python application. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

base_image.description: The base image to use for the Dockerfile, representing the starting point for the build.

maintainer.description: The name of the maintainer or author of the Dockerfile.

expose_port.description: The port number that the container should expose. This is typically the port that the application listens on.

entrypoint.description: The command that will be executed when the Docker container starts.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

message.content:
Below is a **complete, ready‑to‑use set of files** that you can drop into the `nodejs-welcome` repository.  
I’ve written them based on a typical Node.js project layout (e.g. `package.json`, `app.js`, `src/…`).  
If your repo differs slightly, just adjust the paths or names accordingly.

---

## 1️⃣  Dockerfile

```dockerfile
# Dockerfile
# ------------------------------------
# Base image – choose the one that matches your Node version
# (you can change it to python:3.10-slim if you prefer a Python image)
FROM node:18-alpine

# Maintainer
LABEL maintainer="Your Name <you@example.com>"

# Set working directory
WORKDIR /usr/src/app

# Install dependencies
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci --only=production

# Copy source code
COPY . .

# Expose the port your app listens on
EXPOSE 3000

# Start the application
CMD ["npm", "start"]
```

> **Why this Dockerfile?**  
> * `node:18-alpine` is small, fast, and contains the Node runtime.  
> * `npm ci` guarantees a reproducible install from `package-lock.json`.  
> * The app is started with `npm start` – make sure your `package.json` has a `"start"` script that runs the server (e.g. `"node app.js"`).  
> * Port `3000` is the default for many Node apps; change it if your app uses a different port.

---

## 2️⃣  Kubernetes YAMLs

Create a file called `k8s/deployment.yaml` (or any name you prefer).  
It contains both the Deployment and the Service.

```yaml
# k8s/deployment.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-deployment
  labels:
    app: nodejs-welcome
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-welcome
        image: ghcr.io/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest   # <-- will be built by GitHub Actions
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
        env:
        - name: NODE_ENV
          value: production
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-service
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 80
    targetPort: 3000
```

> **What this does**  
> * Deploys 2 replicas of your app.  
> * Exposes the container’s port 3000 to the cluster via a Service on port 80.  
> * Uses the image that will be pushed to GitHub Container Registry (`ghcr.io/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest`).  
> * You can change `replicas`, `image`, or `port` as needed.

---

## 3️⃣  GitHub Actions Workflow

Create a file at `.github/workflows/docker-build.yml`:

```yaml
# .github/workflows/docker-build.yml
name: Build & Push Docker Image

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
      # Checkout the repo
      - name: Checkout repository
        uses: actions/checkout@v4

      # Log in to GitHub Container Registry
      - name: Log in to GHCR
        uses: docker/login-action@v3
        with:
          registry: ghcr.io
          username: ${{ github.actor }}
          password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}

      # Build the Docker image
      - name: Build Docker image
        run: |
          docker build \
            --tag ghcr.io/${{ github.repository_owner }}/nodejs-welcome:latest \
            --tag ghcr.io/${{ github.repository_owner }}/nodejs-welcome:${{ github.sha }} \
            .

      # Push the image
      - name: Push Docker image
        run: |
          docker push ghcr.io/${{ github.repository_owner }}/nodejs-welcome:latest
          docker push ghcr.io/${{ github.repository_owner }}/nodejs-welcome:${{ github.sha }}

      # Optional: Update the Kubernetes manifests with the new image tag
      # (requires a separate step or a tool like `yq` if you want to automate it)
```

> **Key points**  
> * Uses the built‑in `GITHUB_TOKEN` to authenticate to GHCR.  
> * Tags the image with `latest` and the commit SHA for traceability.  
> * Pushes both tags to the registry.  
> * If you want the Kubernetes YAML to automatically reference the new SHA, you can add a step that edits the YAML (e.g. with `yq`) and commits the change back to the repo.

---

## 4️⃣  Commit & Push

Once you have added the files above to your local clone, run:

```bash
# 1. Add the new files
git add Dockerfile k8s/deployment.yaml .github/workflows/docker-build.yml

# 2. Commit
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests, and CI workflow"

# 3. Push to main
git push origin main
```

> **Tip** – If you’re on a branch other than `main`, replace `main` with your branch name.  
> After pushing, the GitHub Actions workflow will automatically run, build the image, and push it to GHCR.

---

### Quick sanity check

1. **Dockerfile** – `docker build -t test .` should succeed locally.  
2. **K8s** – `kubectl apply -f k8s/deployment.yaml` should deploy the pods.  
3. **GitHub Actions** – After pushing, check the Actions tab to confirm the job succeeded.

---

That’s it! Drop those files into the repo, commit, push, and you’ll have a fully automated Docker build pipeline and ready‑to‑deploy Kubernetes manifests. Happy coding!
